The ReCARES Network.intro: ReCARES collects donated medical equipment and supplies and redistributes them through sites in San Francisco, Oakland and Marin.
reasons: Equipment that one household no longer needs can help another person move around, manage daily care or leave home more independently.
Donated goods and volunteer effort allow the network to serve people with a relatively small operating budget.
Three local distribution sites offer a practical route to people who might otherwise face cost or access barriers.
reservations: The number of people gaining safe, useful equipment they would not otherwise obtain—and how long it helps them—is not yet measured.
The amount of additional distribution a new donation would fund is unverified; donated equipment and volunteer capacity also matter.
The ReCARES Network.cost: Our central estimate is about $75,000 per better life (10 Bay Area QALYs). The separate weighted-scenario estimate is about $108,000. Both depend on uncertain assumptions about additional access, safe use and duration of benefit.

Breathe California.intro: Breathe California supports lung health through smoking-cessation counseling, asthma home visits, respiratory-equipment access, education and clean-air work.
reasons: Helping people stop smoking or obtain effective respiratory care can improve health when comparable care would otherwise be delayed or missed.
The organization combines individual support with work on the environmental conditions that affect breathing.
Current services and newer tax filings provide evidence that the organization continues to operate.
reservations: Public information does not establish how many additional patients complete effective care because of a new donation.
Our health model does not capture all potential environmental and policy benefits, and the allocation of additional funding is uncertain.
Breathe California.cost: The central estimate for the clinical benefits we can model is $10.75 million per 10 Bay Area QALYs. It includes the full donation cost but not every possible benefit of the organization; it is not a complete measure of its social value.

SPUR.intro: SPUR researches and advocates for better housing, transportation and public institutions across the Bay Area. Its staff develop policy proposals, support implementation and convene public agencies and other organizations. Recent work includes permitting reform, transit funding and cleaner household appliances.
reasons: Improving public decisions can reach people beyond the scale of a direct-service program.
Earlier housing and more useful transit can improve daily life and reduce actual household expenses.
Published policy analyses and financial disclosures make its work and organizational costs open to examination.
reservations: Adopted zoning and funded transit plans are already the baseline; a new donation cannot receive credit for those entire reforms.
Additional occupied homes, service hours, health improvements and household savings per donation are judgment assumptions, not measured SPUR-specific effects.
Funding response, recipient incidence and the value of other institutional work remain uncertain; this is not a verified marginal funding offer.
SPUR.cost: We estimate $13.01M per better life in the Bay Area under a conditional health-and-household-resource scenario. An illustrative $10,000 comparison supports two accelerated occupied-home courses, 20 additional useful transit service-hours and one accelerated appliance household. The possible benefits are earlier stable homes, better access and lower actual expenses—not the value of buildings, public loan principal or regional GDP.

GLIDE Foundation.intro: GLIDE Foundation provides meals, housing assistance, family support and access to health services in San Francisco. Its health team connects people to public-partner treatment, testing and practical support. This report examines a donation to the Foundation, keeping its separate Church and partner services distinct.
reasons: Practical services can reach people facing several barriers to food, housing and treatment at the same time.
Connections to medication treatment and housing stabilization offer plausible, concrete health pathways.
Household relief from food, rent and childcare can matter in addition to clinical health, and published financial disclosures allow scrutiny of costs.
reservations: Additional completed services attributable to another donation are not established by reported activity counts.
The outcome and household-income assumptions are judgments rather than measured GLIDE-specific causal effects.
Owner, taxpayer, benefit-cliff, policy and other portfolio effects remain unquantified; the calculation is not a verified funding offer.
GLIDE Foundation.cost: Our conditional estimate is $14.40M per better life in the Bay Area. A $100,000 comparison models additional rescue support, treatment access, food, housing and family courses, with separate health and signed household-resource effects. Native course costs and donor response are assumptions; these are not services a donor can buy at a guaranteed price.

HOPE Pacifica.intro: HOPE supports community naloxone access, overdose-prevention education and family resources through a local distribution network.
reasons: Having naloxone nearby can make a critical difference during an opioid overdose.
A community organization may solve practical access and stocking problems that remain even when medication is publicly supplied.
Named distribution sites provide a concrete local service to investigate.
reservations: We have not verified original annual expenses, unique people protected or a priced plan for additional capacity; these gaps prevent a giving recommendation.
Public programs also supply medication and distribution hardware, so the additional contribution of a donation needs to be established.
HOPE Pacifica.cost: The central scenario is about $555,000 per 10 Bay Area QALYs; the separate signed scenario mixture is about $763,000. These are exploratory calculations using assumed budgets and delivery effects, not measured returns.

Housing Action Coalition.intro: Housing Action Coalition works on housing production, project assistance and implementation education. Its Developer Pathway Program offers technical support for emerging housing practitioners. This report assesses an explicitly designated charitable gift to the c3 entity, not default membership in its affiliated advocacy entity.
reasons: Helping viable projects reach occupancy sooner could improve housing conditions and affordability.
Technical assistance provides a more concrete delivery mechanism than treating every policy announcement as additional housing.
Published returns and program descriptions allow scrutiny of organizational boundaries, spending and current activity.
reservations: The current Developer Pathway Program is sponsored and applications are closed; an additional funding tranche is not verified.
Project completion, occupancy acceleration and household outcomes attributable to another gift remain judgment assumptions.
Charitable and advocacy finances are not consolidated, and wider institutional benefits and comprehensive costs remain unquantified.
Housing Action Coalition.cost: Our conditional estimate is $238.60M per better life in the Bay Area, including health and signed household-resource effects. An illustrative $100,000 comparison models 0.576 advisory-supported and 1.8 implementation-related accelerated occupied-home equivalents, with finite catchup periods. This is not evidence that those homes or a particular donation opportunity are available.

Project Homeless Connect.intro: Project Homeless Connect helps people experiencing homelessness access practical services, including routes to glasses, hearing care and dentures.
reasons: Corrective care can make it easier to see, communicate, eat and manage daily life.
Help with appointments, prescriptions, fitting and follow-up can matter even when treatment is covered by insurance.
Named clinical partners and documented service events provide concrete routes from navigation to completed care.
reservations: Current completed-care counts, project spending and the capacity funded by an additional donation remain unresolved.
The health estimates transfer evidence from other settings and rely on uncertain assumptions about care that would otherwise be missed.
Project Homeless Connect.cost: The central estimate is about $774,000 per 10 Bay Area QALYs in donor cost, or $1.08 million with a gross allowance for associated outside resources. These are conditional estimates, not verified prices for additional treatment.

Pacific Hearing Connection.intro: Pacific Hearing Connection offers reduced-fee hearing assessments, hearing aids and follow-up in the Bay Area. Donated devices, professional time and space help support access. It also provides outreach and education.
reasons: Appropriately fitted hearing aids can improve communication for people who would otherwise remain untreated.
Donated devices, professional time and space can help make care more affordable.
An operating service and named clinical leadership provide a practical local route to treatment.
reservations: Additional offers, completed fittings, continued use and equivalent alternatives are not established by a reconciled patient ledger.
Clinical benefits depend on utility measurement, discontinuation, later alternative care and donor responsiveness.
Fees, access costs and maintenance can offset household savings; complete external costs and additional funding capacity remain unknown.
Pacific Hearing Connection.cost: We estimate about $9.72M per better life in the Bay Area, including health and signed household-resource benefits. A $10,000 comparison models about 1.43 additional paired-person offers, 1.13 fittings and 0.55 initial useful users without equivalent alternative care. Hearing gains improve communication, while fees and maintenance reduce the combined benefit. These are planning judgments, not a current treatment quote.

North East Medical Services.intro: North East Medical Services provides primary and specialty care, pharmacy, dental care and other health services, with culturally and linguistically responsive care.
reasons: Language and access barriers can prevent people from receiving effective care; responsive services can help bridge that gap.
Existing liver-health services offer a plausible way to reconnect people with chronic hepatitis B monitoring and indicated treatment.
Clinical infrastructure provides a concrete starting point for investigating additional patient follow-up.
reservations: The official donation recipient is a separate Foundation; a general donation has not been linked to additional hepatitis B care.
The conditional navigation model relies on uncertain evidence transfer and does not establish the impact of ordinary Foundation giving.
North East Medical Services.cost: Bay Area health impact per general donation remains unestimated. The separate conditional navigation model is about $1.20 million per 10 QALYs and requires a specific long-term funding commitment; it is not a price for an unrestricted donation.

Friends of the Urban Forest.intro: Friends of the Urban Forest plants and cares for San Francisco street trees, installs sidewalk gardens and runs community and workforce programs.
reasons: Street trees can improve neighborhood conditions through shade, greenery and opportunities for outdoor activity.
Planting and establishment care offer a tangible route to lasting benefits, especially in neighborhoods with little tree cover.
Its annual planting and care reports provide concrete delivery evidence that can be checked against city records.
reservations: Health benefits per surviving local tree are not directly measured; our QALY assumptions remain judgments.
Publicly funded work is a substantial baseline, and new plantings do not establish what an extra donation adds.
Friends of the Urban Forest.cost: The central estimate is about $1.65 million per 10 Bay Area QALYs. The separate weighted illustration is about $942,000 and depends heavily on a favorable scenario. Neither establishes current room for additional funding.
